name: Fox Kitten
summary: Fox Kitten is threat actor with a suspected nexus to the Iranian government that has been active since at least 2017 against entities in the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, Australia, and North America. Fox Kitten has targeted multiple industrial verticals including oil and gas, technology, government, defense, healthcare, manufacturing, and engineering.

procedures.text: Fox Kitten has created KeyBase accounts to communicate with ransomware victims.
Fox Kitten has used a Twitter account to communicate with ransomware victims.
Fox Kitten has used valid credentials with various services during lateral movement.
Fox Kitten has exploited known vulnerabilities in Fortinet, PulseSecure, and Palo Alto VPN appliances.
Fox Kitten has used cmd.exe likely as a password changing mechanism.
Fox Kitten has used Scheduled Tasks for persistence and to load and execute a reverse proxy binary.
Fox Kitten has used PowerShell scripts to access credential data.
Fox Kitten has used a Perl reverse shell to communicate with C2.
SystemBC: SystemBC has leveraged VBScript to execute malicious code.
SystemBC: SystemBC has utilized native Windows API functions such as `EnumWindows`and `GetVolumeInformationA` during discovery activities.
PsExec: Microsoft Sysinternals PsExec is a popular administration tool that can be used to execute binaries on remote systems using a temporary Windows service.
Fox Kitten has installed web shells on compromised hosts to maintain access.
Fox Kitten has created a local user account with administrator privileges.
Fox Kitten has used sticky keys to launch a command prompt.
PsExec: PsExec has the ability to remotely create accounts on target systems.
PsExec: PsExec can leverage Windows services to escalate privileges from administrator to SYSTEM with the `-s` argument.
Fox Kitten has base64 encoded scripts to avoid detection.
Fox Kitten has base64 encoded payloads to avoid detection.
Fox Kitten has named the task for a reverse proxy lpupdate to appear legitimate.
Fox Kitten has named binaries and configuration files svhost and dllhost respectively to appear legitimate.
China Chopper: China Chopper's client component is packed with UPX.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key can remove its log file from disk.
China Chopper: China Chopper's server component can change the timestamp of files.

SystemBC: SystemBC has the ability to decrypt RC4 encrypted packets and to decode obfuscated data before C2 communication. Additionally, SystemBC has decrypted its config file that was encoded with XOR and a hardcoded 40-byte key.

SystemBC: SystemBC has checked if the last characters of DNS server names end in.bit before initializing C2 communication. SystemBC has identified running processes associated with anti-virus solutions to include `a2guard.exe` to determine whether it executes or not.
SystemBC: SystemBC has utilized the `-WindowStyle Hidden -ep bypass -file `to conceal PowerShell windows.
SystemBC: SystemBC has downloaded a text file into memory and set the area of memory via the VirtualProtect call. Then, SystemBC has executed the file via the CreateThread call.

SystemBC: SystemBC has leveraged the Sleep functions before and after commands to ensure execution using the hexadecimal values within commands to include `Sleep(0x2710u)` that waits 10 seconds, and `Sleep(0xEA60u)` for 60 seconds.
Fox Kitten has used prodump to dump credentials from LSASS.
Fox Kitten has used Volume Shadow Copy to access credential information from NTDS.
Fox Kitten has brute forced RDP credentials.
Fox Kitten has accessed files to gain valid credentials.
Fox Kitten has used scripts to access credential information from the KeePass database.
China Chopper: China Chopper's server component can perform brute force password guessing against authentication portals.
Fox Kitten has used tools including NMAP to conduct broad scanning to identify open ports.
Fox Kitten has used WizTree to obtain network files and directory listings.
Fox Kitten has accessed ntuser.dat and UserClass.dat on compromised hosts.
Fox Kitten has accessed Registry hives ntuser.dat and UserClass.dat.
Fox Kitten has used Angry IP Scanner to detect remote systems.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key has the ability to gather the hostname of the victim machine.
Fox Kitten has used the Softerra LDAP browser to browse documentation on service accounts.
Fox Kitten has used Google Chrome bookmarks to identify internal resources and assets.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key can identify the IP and MAC addresses of the compromised host.
SystemBC: SystemBC has the ability to enumerate running processes.

SystemBC: SystemBC has leveraged the time of the device to create a text file with a filename that uses the function of `uniqid(time()).‘.txt`, consisting of the 10 character UNIX timestamp and 13 hexadecimal characters.
Fox Kitten has used valid accounts to access SMB shares.
Fox Kitten has used RDP to log in and move laterally in the target environment.
Fox Kitten has used the PuTTY and Plink tools for lateral movement.
Fox Kitten has installed TightVNC server and client on compromised servers and endpoints for lateral movement.
Fox Kitten has exploited known vulnerabilities in remote services including RDP.
PsExec: PsExec can be used to download or upload a file over a network share.
Fox Kitten has searched local system resources to access sensitive documents.
Fox Kitten has searched network shares to access sensitive documents.
Fox Kitten has accessed victim security and IT environments and Microsoft Teams to mine valuable information.
Fox Kitten has obtained files from the victim's cloud storage instances.
Fox Kitten has used 7-Zip to archive data.
Fox Kitten has downloaded additional tools including PsExec directly to endpoints.
Fox Kitten has used the open source reverse proxy tools including FRPC and Go Proxy to establish connections from C2 to local servers.
Fox Kitten has used Amazon Web Services to host C2.
Fox Kitten has used protocol tunneling for communication and RDP activity on compromised hosts through the use of open source tools such as ngrok and custom tool SSHMinion.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key has sent its public key to the C2 server over TCP.
SystemBC: SystemBC has encoded with XOR and encrypted with RC4 its beacon.
China Chopper: China Chopper's server component executes code sent via HTTP POST commands.
SystemBC: SystemBC has used DNS servers to resolve.bit domains to C2 infrastructure.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key has designated machines in the compromised network to serve as reverse proxy pivot points to channel communications with C2.

SystemBC: SystemBC has used multiple proxy layers, such as SOCKS5 and Tor, for C2 communication. SystemBC has also leveraged Tor for encrypting and concealing C2 traffic. The server component of SystemBC has used SOCKS5 for C2 communication.
ngrok: ngrok can provide DGA for C2 servers through the use of random URL strings that change every 12 hours.
SystemBC: The server component of SystemBC has used various TCP ports for C2 communication.
SystemBC: SystemBC has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key has used RSA encrypted communications with C2.
ngrok: ngrok has been used by threat actors to configure servers for data exfiltration.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key can encrypt data on victim's machines using RSA and AES algorithms in order to extort a ransom payment for decryption.
Pay2Key: Pay2Key can stop the MS SQL service at the end of the encryption process to release files locked by the service.
